records.source: וַיֵּ֥רֶד שִׁמְשׁ֖וֹן תִּמְנָ֑תָה וַיַּ֥רְא אִשָּׁ֛ה בְּתִמְנָ֖תָה מִבְּנ֥וֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים׃
records.gloss: And went down Samson to Timnah, and he saw a woman in Timnah from [the] daughters of [the] Philistines.
pieces: Samson went down to Timnah, and in Timnah he noticed one of the young Philistine women.

L.1: And Samson went down to Timnah, and he saw a woman in Timnah from the daughters of the Philistines.

R.1: Samson went down to the town of Timnah. While he was there, he saw a young Philistine woman.

decisions.choice: went down to Timnah: from the hill country down into the valley
decisions.reason: Samson's home was at Zorah and Eshtaol in the hills (13:2, 25). Timnah lay lower, toward the plain, on the border between Judah and Dan (Joshua 15:10; 19:43), so the story speaks of going "down" to it and "up" from it (verse 2).

decisions.choice: the daughters of the Philistines: young Philistine women
decisions.reason: "Daughters" of a people means the women of that people, here young women of marriageable age. The phrase sets the scene: the woman Samson wants is a Philistine, from the people who ruled Israel at this time (13:1).

decisions.choice: the town of Timnah
decisions.reason: Readable adds "the town of" so that a new reader knows Timnah is a place.

records.heading: Samson and the woman of Timnah

records.source: וַיַּ֗עַל וַיַּגֵּד֙ לְאָבִ֣יו וּלְאִמּ֔וֹ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אִשָּׁ֛ה רָאִ֥יתִי בְתִמְנָ֖תָה מִבְּנ֣וֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וְעַתָּ֕ה קְחוּ־אוֹתָ֥הּ לִּ֖י לְאִשָּֽׁה׃
records.gloss: And he went up and told his father and his mother, and he said, a woman I have seen in Timnah from [the] daughters of [the] Philistines; and now take her for me as a wife.
pieces: He came back up and told his father and mother, "I have seen a woman in Timnah, one of the young Philistine women. Now get her for me as my wife."

L.2: And he went up and told his father and his mother, and he said, "A woman I have seen in Timnah from the daughters of the Philistines; and now take her for me as a wife."

R.2: When he came back home, he told his father and mother, "I saw a young Philistine woman in Timnah. Now go and arrange for me to marry her."

decisions.choice: take her for me as a wife: the parents arrange the marriage
decisions.reason: Marriages were arranged between families, and the groom's family made the agreement with the bride's father, often with a payment to him (Genesis 34:4, 8-12; Exodus 22:15-16). The command is plural: Samson tells both parents to make the arrangements.

decisions.choice: A woman I have seen: the woman comes first for emphasis
decisions.reason: Samson puts "a woman" at the head of his sentence. What he has seen is what drives him, a theme of the chapter (verses 1, 3, 7).

decisions.choice: go and arrange for me to marry her
decisions.reason: "Take her for me" means "arrange the marriage for me". Readable says so, so that it does not sound as if the parents are to fetch the woman by force.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר ל֜וֹ אָבִ֣יו וְאִמּ֗וֹ הַאֵין֩ בִּבְנ֨וֹת אַחֶ֤יךָ וּבְכָל־עַמִּי֙ אִשָּׁ֔ה כִּֽי־אַתָּ֤ה הוֹלֵךְ֙ לָקַ֣חַת אִשָּׁ֔ה מִפְּלִשְׁתִּ֖ים הָעֲרֵלִ֑ים וַיֹּ֨אמֶר שִׁמְשׁ֤וֹן אֶל־אָבִיו֙ אוֹתָ֣הּ קַֽח־לִ֔י כִּֽי־הִ֖יא יָשְׁרָ֥ה בְעֵינָֽי׃
records.gloss: And said to him his father and his mother, [is there] not among [the] daughters of your brothers and among all my people a woman, that you [are] going to take a wife from the Philistines the uncircumcised? And said Samson to his father, her take for me, for she [is] right in my eyes.
pieces: His father and mother said to him, "Is there not a woman among your relatives or anywhere among my people? Must you go and take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me. She is the one who looks right to me."

L.3: And his father and his mother said to him, "Is there no woman among the daughters of your brothers, or among all my people, that you are going to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" And Samson said to his father, "Her take for me, for she is right in my eyes."

R.3: His father and mother said to him, "Is there no woman among our relatives or among all our people? Why do you have to go and marry one of the Philistines? They are not even circumcised!" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me. She is the one I like."

decisions.choice: the uncircumcised Philistines: outsiders to Israel's covenant
decisions.reason: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham's family (Genesis 17:10-14). The Philistines did not practice it, so "uncircumcised" marks them as outside that covenant; it is a term of contempt (1 Samuel 14:6; 17:26). Israel had been warned against marrying into the peoples around it (Exodus 34:16; Deuteronomy 7:3; Judges 3:6).

decisions.choice: she is right in my eyes: she pleases me
decisions.reason: The phrase means "she is the one I want". It is the phrase of the book's closing verdict, "each did what was right in his own eyes" (17:6; 21:25): Samson chooses by what he sees and likes, as verses 1 and 7 also show.

decisions.choice: my people: one parent speaks for both
decisions.reason: Both parents are named as speaking, but the text says "my people", not "our people". It is one voice speaking for the two of them; the sense is the people of Israel.

decisions.choice: Her take for me: "her" comes first
decisions.reason: Samson puts "her" at the front, against his parents' question: not some other woman, but this one.

decisions.choice: looks right to me / the one I like
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of seeing, which links this verse with 17:6 and 21:25; Readable says plainly that Samson likes her.

decisions.choice: our relatives, our people; They are not even circumcised!
decisions.reason: Readable uses "our" because both parents speak, and turns "the uncircumcised Philistines" into a short exclamation that carries the parents' dismay.

records.source: וְאָבִ֨יו וְאִמּ֜וֹ לֹ֣א יָדְע֗וּ כִּ֤י מֵיְהוָה֙ הִ֔יא כִּי־תֹאֲנָ֥ה הֽוּא־מְבַקֵּ֖שׁ מִפְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וּבָעֵ֣ת הַהִ֔יא פְּלִשְׁתִּ֖ים מֹשְׁלִ֥ים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ
records.gloss: And his father and his mother not knew that from Yahweh [was] it, for an occasion he [was] seeking from the Philistines. And at the time the that, [the] Philistines [were] ruling over Israel.
pieces: His father and mother did not know that this came from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, for {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was looking for an opportunity to act against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.

L.4: And his father and his mother did not know that it [was] from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, for {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} [was] seeking an occasion against the Philistines. And at that time the Philistines [were] ruling over Israel.

R.4: His father and mother did not know that this came from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} was looking for a reason to move against the Philistines, who were ruling over Israel at that time.

decisions.choice: it was from the LORD: God was at work in Samson's choice
decisions.reason: The narrator tells the reader what the parents could not see: God was working through Samson's wish to marry a Philistine to bring about conflict with Israel's rulers. Scripture speaks the same way elsewhere of God working through human choices (Joshua 11:20; 1 Kings 12:15). This does not make the choice right; verse 3 has shown it was against what Israel was taught.

decisions.choice: he was seeking: the LORD
decisions.reason: "He" most naturally refers to the LORD, just named: God was seeking an occasion. It could also refer to Samson, looking for a reason to quarrel with the Philistines, but the sentence explains why the matter was "from the LORD", which fits God as the one seeking.

decisions.choice: an occasion: an opening, a pretext for a quarrel
decisions.reason: The noun occurs only here; a related verb is used in 2 Kings 5:7 of a king "seeking a quarrel". It is an occasion for conflict with the Philistines.

decisions.choice: the Philistines were ruling over Israel
decisions.reason: The Philistines had held Israel for forty years (13:1). There is no war in this story; Israel lives under them, which is why the conflict has to begin with one man.

decisions.choice: The LORD was looking
decisions.reason: Readable names the LORD instead of "he", following the reading in m2.

records.source: וַיֵּ֧רֶד שִׁמְשׁ֛וֹן וְאָבִ֥יו וְאִמּ֖וֹ תִּמְנָ֑תָה וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ עַד־כַּרְמֵ֣י תִמְנָ֔תָה וְהִנֵּה֙ כְּפִ֣יר אֲרָי֔וֹת שֹׁאֵ֖ג לִקְרָאתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And went down Samson and his father and his mother to Timnah, and they came to [the] vineyards of Timnah, and look, a young lion of lions roaring to meet him.
pieces: Then Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. When they reached the vineyards of Timnah, a young lion suddenly came at him, roaring.

L.5: And Samson and his father and his mother went down to Timnah, and they came to the vineyards of Timnah, and look, a young lion of [the] lions [was] roaring to meet him.

R.5: Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. Near the vineyards of Timnah, a young lion suddenly came roaring at Samson.

decisions.choice: his parents went too, but the lion met Samson alone
decisions.reason: The parents travel with him, yet the lion comes "to meet him", and verse 6 says he did not tell them what happened. The text does not explain it; Samson must have been apart from them for a time, for example among the vineyards.

decisions.choice: a young lion of lions: a young lion in its full strength
decisions.reason: The word means a young lion that hunts for itself, past the cub stage and at its most dangerous (Ezekiel 19:2-3). "Of lions" stresses that it was a real lion.

decisions.choice: the vineyards of Timnah
decisions.reason: Samson was a Nazirite from birth (13:5, 7), and a Nazirite was to keep away from wine and from everything that comes from the vine (Numbers 6:3-4; Judges 13:14). The narrator places him among vineyards without comment.

decisions.choice: suddenly
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "look!" marks something sudden and unexpected; Balanced and Readable say "suddenly".

records.heading: The lion and the riddle

records.source: וַתִּצְלַ֨ח עָלָ֜יו ר֣וּחַ יְהוָ֗ה וַֽיְשַׁסְּעֵ֨הוּ֙ כְּשַׁסַּ֣ע הַגְּדִ֔י וּמְא֖וּמָה אֵ֣ין בְּיָד֑וֹ וְלֹ֤א הִגִּיד֙ לְאָבִ֣יו וּלְאִמּ֔וֹ אֵ֖ת אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָֽׂה׃
records.gloss: And rushed on him [the] Spirit of Yahweh, and he tore it as tearing the kid, and anything not [was] in his hand; and not he told his father and his mother what he had done.
pieces: The Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} rushed on him, and with nothing in his hands he ripped the lion apart as easily as one rips apart a young goat. Yet he told neither his father nor his mother what he had done.

L.6: And the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} rushed on him, and he tore it apart as one tears apart a young goat, and there was nothing in his hand; and he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.

R.6: The Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} rushed on Samson. He had no weapon, but he tore the lion apart as easily as tearing apart a little goat. He kept what he had done a secret from his father and mother.

decisions.choice: rushed on him: came on him suddenly and with force
decisions.reason: The verb means to rush or break through. It is used of the Spirit coming on Samson again in 14:19 and 15:14, and on Saul and David (1 Samuel 10:6, 10; 11:6; 16:13). It is stronger than "was on him" (3:10; 11:29).

decisions.choice: the Spirit of the LORD: God's power giving strength
decisions.reason: As with the other judges (3:10; 6:34; 11:29), the Spirit of the LORD gives strength beyond the ordinary. In Samson's case it shows as bodily strength; his strength is God's gift, not his own (13:25; 16:20).

decisions.choice: as one tears a young goat: with ease
decisions.reason: A young goat is a small animal; the comparison shows how little effort it took Samson to tear apart a lion. "Nothing in his hand" means he had no weapon.

decisions.choice: he did not tell his father or his mother
decisions.reason: His silence is what makes the riddle impossible to guess (verses 9, 14, 16).

decisions.choice: as easily as
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out the point of the comparison (m3).

decisions.choice: with nothing in his hands / He had no weapon
decisions.reason: "Nothing in his hand" is put in common English.

records.source: וַיֵּ֖רֶד וַיְדַבֵּ֣ר לָאִשָּׁ֑ה וַתִּישַׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י שִׁמְשֽׁוֹן׃
records.gloss: And he went down and spoke to the woman, and she was right in [the] eyes of Samson.
pieces: Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she looked right to Samson.

L.7: And he went down and spoke to the woman, and she was right in the eyes of Samson.

R.7: Then Samson went on down and talked with the woman. He liked her.

decisions.choice: she was right in Samson's eyes: he was pleased with her
decisions.reason: The same phrase as in verse 3 (see the note there), now said by the narrator: having talked with her, Samson is pleased with his choice.

decisions.choice: spoke to the woman
decisions.reason: Samson now speaks with her himself; in verses 1-3 he had only seen her. The marriage agreement itself is made by his father (verse 10).

decisions.choice: looked right to / He liked her
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

records.source: וַיָּ֤שָׁב מִיָּמִים֙ לְקַחְתָּ֔הּ וַיָּ֣סַר לִרְא֔וֹת אֵ֖ת מַפֶּ֣לֶת הָאַרְיֵ֑ה וְהִנֵּ֨ה עֲדַ֧ת דְּבוֹרִ֛ים בִּגְוִיַּ֥ת הָאַרְיֵ֖ה וּדְבָֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And he returned after days to take her, and he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and look, a swarm of bees [was] in [the] body of the lion, and honey.
pieces: Some time later he went back to marry her, and he turned aside to look at the lion's carcass. There in the lion's body was a swarm of bees, and honey.

L.8: And he returned after [some] days to take her, and he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and look, a swarm of bees [was] in the body of the lion, and honey.

R.8: Some time later Samson went back to marry her. On the way he left the road to look at the dead lion. Inside the lion's body he found a swarm of bees and some honey.

decisions.choice: after days: some time later
decisions.reason: "After days" is an unspecified time. The same word "days" can stand for a year (1 Samuel 1:21; Judges 11:40), and enough time had passed for the carcass to dry out and for bees to make honey, but the text gives no exact length.

decisions.choice: to take her: to marry her
decisions.reason: "Take" a woman is the usual way of saying "marry" (verse 2).

decisions.choice: a swarm of bees and honey in the carcass
decisions.reason: Wild bees make their nests in hollow places. By now the carcass had dried in the heat, and a swarm had settled in it and made honey. The word for "carcass" means "what has fallen"; the second word, "body", is used of a dead body (1 Samuel 31:10).

decisions.choice: On the way he left the road
decisions.reason: "Turned aside" means he went off his route; Readable says so.

records.source: וַיִּרְדֵּ֣הוּ אֶל־כַּפָּ֗יו וַיֵּ֤לֶךְ הָלוֹךְ֙ וְאָכֹ֔ל וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֶל־אָבִ֣יו וְאֶל־אִמּ֔וֹ וַיִּתֵּ֥ן לָהֶ֖ם וַיֹּאכֵ֑לוּ וְלֹֽא־הִגִּ֣יד לָהֶ֔ם כִּ֛י מִגְּוִיַּ֥ת הָאַרְיֵ֖ה רָדָ֥ה הַדְּבָֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And he scraped it into his palms, and he went, going and eating, and he went to his father and to his mother, and he gave to them, and they ate; and not he told them that from [the] body of the lion he had scraped the honey.
pieces: He scooped the honey out into his hands and went on, eating as he walked. When he reached his father and mother, he gave them some, and they ate. Yet he did not tell them he had scooped the honey out of the lion's carcass.

L.9: And he scraped it into his palms and went on, going and eating, and he came to his father and to his mother and gave [some] to them, and they ate; but he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey out of the body of the lion.

R.9: He scooped some honey into his hands and walked on, eating it. When he got back to his father and mother, he gave them some, and they ate it too. But he did not say that the honey came from the dead lion's body.

decisions.choice: scraped: scooped out
decisions.reason: The verb, used here twice, means to scrape or scoop something out. Samson takes the comb out with his hands.

decisions.choice: honey from a carcass
decisions.reason: Touching a dead animal made a person unclean (Leviticus 11:24-25, 39), and a Nazirite was to keep away from the dead (Numbers 6:6). The narrator makes no comment, but his silence before his parents, who also eat, suggests Samson knew they would object.

decisions.choice: he did not tell them
decisions.reason: The second time the narrator says this (verse 6). No one but Samson knows where the honey came from, which is the secret of the riddle in verse 14.

decisions.choice: scooped ... into his hands
decisions.reason: "Palms" in the Hebrew; "hands" is the common English word.

records.source: וַיֵּ֥רֶד אָבִ֖יהוּ אֶל־הָאִשָּׁ֑ה וַיַּ֨עַשׂ שָׁ֤ם שִׁמְשׁוֹן֙ מִשְׁתֶּ֔ה כִּ֛י כֵּ֥ן יַעֲשׂ֖וּ הַבַּחוּרִֽים׃
records.gloss: And went down his father to the woman, and made there Samson a feast, for so used to do the young men.
pieces: His father went down to see the woman, and Samson held a feast there, as young men used to do.

L.10: And his father went down to the woman, and Samson made a feast there, for so the young men used to do.

R.10: Then his father went down to Timnah to see the woman's family. Samson gave a wedding feast there, because that was the custom for young men when they married.

decisions.choice: a feast: a wedding feast with drinking
decisions.reason: The word comes from the verb "drink" and names a feast where wine was served. Here it is the wedding feast, which lasted seven days (verse 12; Genesis 29:22, 27). The narrator does not say whether Samson drank, but a Nazirite was to drink no wine (13:4, 7, 14; Numbers 6:3).

decisions.choice: so the young men used to do: the bridegroom's custom
decisions.reason: The narrator explains a custom of an earlier time: the bridegroom gave the feast. The words show the story is told to readers for whom that custom was no longer familiar.

decisions.choice: his father went down
decisions.reason: The father goes to settle the marriage with the woman's family, as Samson asked in verses 2-3.

decisions.choice: to see the woman / to see the woman's family
decisions.reason: "Went down to the woman" means he went to her home to complete the arrangements. Balanced adds "to see"; Readable says it was her family he went to meet.

records.source: וַיְהִ֖י כִּרְאוֹתָ֣ם אוֹת֑וֹ וַיִּקְחוּ֙ שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים מֵֽרֵעִ֔ים וַיִּהְי֖וּ אִתּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And it was, when they saw him, and they took thirty companions, and they were with him.
pieces: When the people there saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.

L.11: And it happened, when they saw him, that they took thirty companions, and they were with him.

R.11: When the Philistines there saw Samson, they chose thirty young men to keep him company.

decisions.choice: when they saw him
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "saw". The ancient Greek translation reads "when they feared him", which in Hebrew is a very similar-looking verb. The Hebrew makes good sense and is followed here; the Greek may reflect the idea that the thirty were also there to watch a dangerous man.

decisions.choice: thirty companions: the bridegroom's attendants
decisions.reason: The bride's town provided young men as the bridegroom's companions at the feast. Their number matters for the wager in verses 12-13 and for the thirty men of verse 19. One of them was his chief friend (verse 20).

decisions.choice: they: the people of Timnah
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not name who chose the companions; it is the bride's people, "the men of the city" of verse 18.

decisions.choice: the people there / the Philistines there
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the unstated subject (m3).

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָהֶם֙ שִׁמְשׁ֔וֹן אָחֽוּדָה־נָּ֥א לָכֶ֖ם חִידָ֑ה אִם־הַגֵּ֣ד תַּגִּידוּ֩ אוֹתָ֨הּ לִ֜י שִׁבְעַ֨ת יְמֵ֤י הַמִּשְׁתֶּה֙ וּמְצָאתֶ֔ם וְנָתַתִּ֤י לָכֶם֙ שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים סְדִינִ֔ים וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֖ים חֲלִפֹ֥ת בְּגָדִֽים׃
records.gloss: And said to them Samson, let me riddle please to you a riddle; if telling you tell it to me [in] the seven days of the feast and find [it] out, and I will give to you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of garments.
pieces: Samson said to them, "Let me give you a riddle. If you can explain it to me during the seven days of the feast and work it out, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of festive clothes.

L.12: And Samson said to them, "Let me pose a riddle to you. If you can really tell it to me in the seven days of the feast and find [it] out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes.

R.12: Samson said to them, "Let me ask you a riddle. The feast lasts seven days. If you can give me the answer before it is over, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of fine clothes.

decisions.choice: a riddle: a puzzling saying to be solved
decisions.reason: Verb and noun come from the same root: literally "let me riddle you a riddle". The word can name any dark or puzzling saying (Numbers 12:8; 1 Kings 10:1; Psalm 49:5); here it is a riddle posed as a wager.

decisions.choice: if you can really tell it
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for emphasis: "if you indeed tell it". "Tell" a riddle means give its answer; "find it out" means solve it.

decisions.choice: linen garments: costly linen clothing
decisions.reason: The word names a fine linen garment, a mark of wealth (Proverbs 31:24; Isaiah 3:23). Its exact shape is not known.

decisions.choice: changes of clothes: fine clothing for special occasions
decisions.reason: "Changes" are sets of clothing worn in place of everyday clothes, given as rich gifts (Genesis 45:22; 2 Kings 5:5, 22-23). The prize is large: a full outfit for each of the thirty.

decisions.choice: pose a riddle
decisions.reason: English has no verb "to riddle" in this sense, so Literal uses "pose a riddle" and the note gives the Hebrew pattern.

decisions.choice: sets of festive clothes / sets of fine clothes
decisions.reason: "Changes of garments" means good clothes to change into; Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: וְאִם־לֹ֣א תוּכְלוּ֮ לְהַגִּ֣יד לִי֒ וּנְתַתֶּ֨ם אַתֶּ֥ם לִי֙ שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים סְדִינִ֔ים וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֖ים חֲלִיפ֣וֹת בְּגָדִ֑ים וַיֹּ֣אמְרוּ ל֔וֹ ח֥וּדָה חִידָתְךָ֖ וְנִשְׁמָעֶֽנָּה׃
records.gloss: And if not you are able to tell me, and you will give, you, to me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of garments. And they said to him, riddle your riddle, and we will hear it.
pieces: But if you cannot tell me, then you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of festive clothes." They said to him, "Tell us your riddle. Let us hear it."

L.13: But if you are not able to tell me, then you will give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes." And they said to him, "Pose your riddle, and let us hear it."

R.13: But if you cannot tell me the answer, then you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of fine clothes." They answered, "Ask your riddle. Let us hear it."

decisions.choice: you will give: "you" stressed
decisions.reason: The Hebrew adds the pronoun "you" to the verb: the wager runs both ways. Samson stands alone against thirty, so if he wins, he gains thirty sets of clothing at once.

decisions.choice: pose your riddle, and let us hear it: a ready acceptance
decisions.reason: The companions accept the wager at once. The verb and noun are again from the same root, as in verse 12.

decisions.choice: Tell us your riddle / Ask your riddle
decisions.reason: As in verse 12.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֗ם מֵהָֽאֹכֵל֙ יָצָ֣א מַאֲכָ֔ל וּמֵעַ֖ז יָצָ֣א מָת֑וֹק וְלֹ֥א יָכְל֛וּ לְהַגִּ֥יד הַחִידָ֖ה שְׁלֹ֥שֶׁת יָמִֽים׃
records.gloss: And he said to them, from the eater came out food, and from [the] strong came out sweet; and not they were able to tell the riddle three days.
pieces: He said to them, \q "From the one who eats came food; \q from the strong one came something sweet." \q For three days they could not explain the riddle.

L.14: And he said to them, \q "From the eater came out food, \q and from [the] strong came out [something] sweet." \q And they were not able to tell the riddle [for] three days.

R.14: So he said to them, \q "Food came out of the eater; \q something sweet came out of the strong." \q For three days they could not figure out the answer.

decisions.choice: the riddle: the lion and the honey
decisions.reason: The eater and the strong one are the lion; the food and the sweet thing are the honey (verses 8-9, 18). No one could guess it, because Samson had told no one what happened (verses 6, 9). The riddle is a trap more than a fair puzzle.

decisions.choice: eater ... food: one root
decisions.reason: "Eater" and "food" are from the same root, "eat", and the two lines balance each other: eater and food, strong and sweet. The riddle is set as a short pair of poetic lines.

decisions.choice: three days: they failed for three days
decisions.reason: After three days the companions still had no answer, which leads to their threat in verse 15 (see the note on "seventh day" there).

decisions.choice: the riddle set in two lines
decisions.reason: The riddle is a pair of short poetic lines, so it is set in lines, with the narrative before and after it as separate lines. Readable puts the subject at the start of each line, in plain English order.

records.source: וַיְהִ֣י׀בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִ֗י וַיֹּאמְר֤וּ לְאֵֽשֶׁת־שִׁמְשׁוֹן֙ פַּתִּ֣י אֶת־אִישֵׁ֗ךְ וְיַגֶּד־לָ֨נוּ֙ אֶת־הַ֣חִידָ֔ה פֶּן־נִשְׂרֹ֥ף אוֹתָ֛ךְ וְאֶת־בֵּ֥ית אָבִ֖יךְ בָּאֵ֑שׁ הַלְיָרְשֵׁ֕נוּ קְרָאתֶ֥ם לָ֖נוּ הֲלֹֽא׃
records.gloss: And it was on the seventh day, and they said to [the] wife of Samson, entice your husband, that he tell us the riddle, lest we burn you and the house of your father with fire; to impoverish us did you invite us? [is it] not?
pieces: On the seventh day they said to Samson's wife, "Coax your husband into telling us the riddle, or we will set fire to you and your father's household. Did you invite us here to rob us? Is that it?"

L.15: And it happened on the seventh day that they said to Samson's wife, "Entice your husband, so that he tells us the riddle, or we will burn you and your father's house with fire. Did you invite us to make us poor? Is it not [so]?"

R.15: On the seventh day they said to Samson's wife, "Trick your husband into telling us the answer to the riddle. If you do not, we will burn you and your father's whole family to death. Did you invite us here just to take everything we own?"

decisions.choice: the seventh day
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "the seventh day". The ancient Greek and Syriac translations have "the fourth day", which fits the "three days" of verse 14 and the seven days of weeping in verse 17. The Hebrew is followed here; it may mean that the companions came to her at the last moment, after she had already been weeping over Samson for days.

decisions.choice: entice: persuade by trickery
decisions.reason: The verb means to coax or seduce someone, often by deceit. The Philistine leaders will use the same verb when they set Delilah on Samson (16:5).

decisions.choice: burn you and your father's house with fire
decisions.reason: "Your father's house" is the whole household. The threat is meant literally, and it is later carried out (15:6).

decisions.choice: did you invite us to impoverish us? Is it not so?
alternatives: did you invite us here to impoverish us?
decisions.reason: The verb means to take someone's possessions or make them poor: losing the wager would cost each of them a set of fine clothes. The last two words are a question tag, "is it not?". With a small change of one letter they would read "here": "did you invite us here?"

decisions.choice: invite us here / to rob us / take everything we own
decisions.reason: "Here" is natural English for an invitation and does not decide the question in m4. Balanced says "rob" and Readable says "take everything we own" for "impoverish"; Readable leaves the question tag in the force of the question.

records.source: וַתֵּבְךְּ֩ אֵ֨שֶׁת שִׁמְשׁ֜וֹן עָלָ֗יו וַתֹּ֨אמֶר֙ רַק־שְׂנֵאתַ֨נִי֙ וְלֹ֣א אֲהַבְתָּ֔נִי הַֽחִידָ֥ה חַ֨דְתָּ֙ לִבְנֵ֣י עַמִּ֔י וְלִ֖י לֹ֣א הִגַּ֑דְתָּה וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָ֗הּ הִנֵּ֨ה לְאָבִ֧י וּלְאִמִּ֛י לֹ֥א הִגַּ֖דְתִּי וְלָ֥ךְ אַגִּֽיד׃
records.gloss: And wept [the] wife of Samson over him, and she said, only you hate me and not you love me; the riddle you have riddled to [the] sons of my people, and to me not you have told [it]. And he said to her, look, to my father and to my mother not I have told, and to you will I tell?
pieces: Samson's wife wept over him and said, "You only hate me; you do not love me at all. You have given my people a riddle, and you have not told me the answer." He said to her, "Look, I have not told even my father or my mother. Why should I tell you?"

L.16: And Samson's wife wept over him and said, "You only hate me, and you do not love me. You have posed the riddle to the sons of my people, and to me you have not told [it]." And he said to her, "Look, to my father and to my mother I have not told [it], and to you should I tell [it]?"

R.16: Samson's wife cried in front of him. "You hate me!" she said. "You do not really love me. You told my people a riddle, but you will not tell me the answer." Samson said to her, "I have not even told my father and mother. Why should I tell you?"

decisions.choice: you only hate me, you do not love me
decisions.reason: She puts it as sharply as she can: his silence proves he does not love her. Delilah will press him in almost the same words (16:15).

decisions.choice: the sons of my people: her countrymen
decisions.reason: The phrase means the men of her own people, the thirty companions. She sets them against herself: he has shared a riddle with them, but will not share its answer with his wife.

decisions.choice: to my father and to my mother ... and to you?
decisions.reason: Samson puts his parents first for emphasis: he has kept the secret even from them, so why should he tell her? His answer treats her as an outsider, which is how she has just accused him of treating her.

decisions.choice: my people
decisions.reason: "Sons of my people" is an idiom for her countrymen; Balanced and Readable say "my people".

records.source: וַתֵּ֤בְךְּ עָלָיו֙ שִׁבְעַ֣ת הַיָּמִ֔ים אֲשֶׁר־הָיָ֥ה לָהֶ֖ם הַמִּשְׁתֶּ֑ה וַיְהִ֣י׀בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִ֗י וַיַּגֶּד־לָהּ֙ כִּ֣י הֱצִיקַ֔תְהוּ וַתַּגֵּ֥ד הַחִידָ֖ה לִבְנֵ֥י עַמָּֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And she wept over him the seven days which was to them the feast; and it was on the seventh day, and he told her, for she pressed him, and she told the riddle to [the] sons of her people.
pieces: She wept over him all through the seven days of their feast. On the seventh day he told her, because she kept pressing him, and she explained the riddle to her people.

L.17: And she wept over him the seven days that the feast lasted for them, and it happened on the seventh day that he told her, because she pressed him hard, and she told the riddle to the sons of her people.

R.17: She cried in front of him for the whole seven days of the feast. On the seventh day he finally told her, because she kept begging him. Then she told the answer to her people.

decisions.choice: the seven days: through the feast
decisions.reason: She wept through the whole feast. With "the seventh day" in verse 15, this means she was already weeping before the companions threatened her; see the note there.

decisions.choice: she pressed him: she wore him down
decisions.reason: The verb means to press hard, to harass. It is used again when Delilah wears Samson down (16:16).

decisions.choice: she told the riddle: she told its answer
decisions.reason: As in verse 12, "tell" a riddle means give its answer.

decisions.choice: kept pressing / finally / kept begging
decisions.reason: The verb describes pressure over time; Balanced and Readable show that with "kept", and Readable adds "finally".

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמְרוּ לוֹ֩ אַנְשֵׁ֨י הָעִ֜יר בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִ֗י בְּטֶ֨רֶם֙ יָבֹ֣א הַחַ֔רְסָה מַה־מָּת֣וֹק מִדְּבַ֔שׁ וּמֶ֥ה עַ֖ז מֵאֲרִ֑י וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֔ם לוּלֵא֙ חֲרַשְׁתֶּ֣ם בְּעֶגְלָתִ֔י לֹ֥א מְצָאתֶ֖ם חִידָתִֽי׃
records.gloss: And said to him [the] men of the city on the seventh day before went the sun, what [is] sweeter than honey, and what [is] stronger than a lion? And he said to them, if not you had plowed with my heifer, not you would have found out my riddle.
pieces: On the seventh day, before the sun went down, the men of the city said to him, \q "What is sweeter than honey? \q What is stronger than a lion?" \q Samson answered them, \q "If you had not plowed with my heifer, \q you would never have worked out my riddle."

L.18: And the men of the city said to him on the seventh day, before the sun went down, \q "What [is] sweeter than honey? \q And what [is] stronger than a lion?" \q And he said to them, \q "If you had not plowed with my heifer, \q you would not have found out my riddle."

R.18: On the seventh day, just before sunset, the men of the town said to Samson, \q "What is sweeter than honey? \q What is stronger than a lion?" \q Samson said to them, \q "If you had not plowed with my young cow, my wife, \q you would never have solved my riddle."

decisions.choice: before the sun went down: just before the deadline
alternatives: before he went into the bridal room
decisions.reason: The word for "sun" here is a rare one (8:13; Job 9:7). The seven days end at sunset, so the men answer at the last possible moment. A small change to the word would give "before he went into the bridal room", but the text as it stands speaks of the sun.

decisions.choice: their answer as two questions
decisions.reason: The men answer the riddle in its own style, with two balanced lines: what is sweeter than honey, what is stronger than a lion. The sweet thing is honey and the strong one is the lion (verse 14).

decisions.choice: plowed with my heifer: used my wife
decisions.reason: A heifer is a young cow, an animal used to plow. Samson's retort says they got the answer by working through his wife, using what was his, as one might use another man's animal without leave. The picture is coarse and contemptuous, of them and of her.

decisions.choice: both sayings set in lines
decisions.reason: The men's answer and Samson's retort are each a pair of poetic lines, so they are set in lines, with the narrative words before each as a line of its own.

decisions.choice: my young cow, my wife
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the picture and adds "my wife" so that a new reader understands it; "never" strengthens the point.

records.source: וַתִּצְלַ֨ח עָלָ֜יו ר֣וּחַ יְהוָ֗ה וַיֵּ֨רֶד אַשְׁקְל֜וֹן וַיַּ֥ךְ מֵהֶ֣ם׀שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים אִ֗ישׁ וַיִּקַּח֙ אֶת־חֲלִ֣יצוֹתָ֔ם וַיִּתֵּן֙ הַחֲלִיפ֔וֹת לְמַגִּידֵ֖י הַחִידָ֑ה וַיִּ֣חַר אַפּ֔וֹ וַיַּ֖עַל בֵּ֥ית אָבִֽיהוּ׃פ
records.gloss: And rushed on him [the] Spirit of Yahweh, and he went down [to] Ashkelon, and he struck of them thirty men, and he took their spoils, and he gave the changes to [the] tellers of the riddle; and burned his anger, and he went up [to the] house of his father.
pieces: Then the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} rushed on him. He went down to Ashkelon, struck down thirty of their men, stripped them of their clothes, and gave the sets of clothing to those who had explained the riddle. Burning with anger, he went back up to his father's house.

L.19: And the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} rushed on him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men of them, and he took what he stripped from them and gave the changes [of clothes] to those who had told the riddle. And his anger burned, and he went up to his father's house.

R.19: Then the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} rushed on Samson. He went down to the Philistine city of Ashkelon and killed thirty of its men. He took their clothes and gave them to the men who had answered the riddle. Samson was very angry, and he went back home to his father's house.

decisions.choice: the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him
decisions.reason: As in verse 6. The same power that tore the lion now drives Samson against the Philistines, the "occasion" of verse 4.

decisions.choice: Ashkelon: a Philistine city on the coast
decisions.reason: Ashkelon was one of the five chief Philistine cities (Joshua 13:3), on the coast more than twenty miles from Timnah. Samson takes the payment from Philistines far from the wedding town.

decisions.choice: their spoils: what is stripped from the dead
decisions.reason: The word means what is stripped off a fallen man, his clothing and gear (2 Samuel 2:21). Samson pays his wager with the clothes of the dead.

decisions.choice: his anger burned: he was furious
decisions.reason: A common Hebrew way to say someone was very angry. He leaves without his wife and goes home.

decisions.choice: the Philistine city of Ashkelon
decisions.reason: Readable says what Ashkelon was.

decisions.choice: stripped them of their clothes / took their clothes
decisions.reason: The spoil here is clothing, as the next clause shows; Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: וַתְּהִ֖י אֵ֣שֶׁת שִׁמְשׁ֑וֹן לְמֵ֣רֵעֵ֔הוּ אֲשֶׁ֥ר רֵעָ֖ה לֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And became [the] wife of Samson [the wife] of his companion who had been a companion to him.
pieces: Then Samson's wife was given to his companion, the one who had served as his best man.

L.20: And Samson's wife became [the wife] of his companion, who had been a companion to him.

R.20: Then Samson's wife was given to the man who had been his best man at the wedding.

decisions.choice: his companion who had been a companion to him: his best man
decisions.reason: The noun is the word for the thirty "companions" (verse 11), and the verb means to act as someone's friend. Here it names the bridegroom's chief friend, the one who attended him at the wedding, much like a best man.

decisions.choice: Samson's wife became his companion's
decisions.reason: Samson had gone home in anger (verse 19). Her father took this to mean he had rejected her and gave her to the companion (15:2). The next chapter tells what followed.

decisions.choice: was given to
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says she "became" his companion's. Balanced and Readable say "was given", since 15:2 shows her father gave her.

decisions.choice: best man
decisions.reason: "Best man" is the nearest English custom to the bridegroom's chief friend.
